summary: At Golgotha Jesus is crucified between two criminals under the title “The King of the Jews,” and, mocked by all, He prays for His executioners and promises Paradise.
key_insight: Rulers, soldiers and a dying criminal all said the same thing: “Save Yourself.” Jesus’ own words in those hours went the other way: a prayer for His executioners, a promise to a dying man and care for His mother.
story: They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull. There they offered Him “wine mingled with myrrh” to drink, {Mk} but when He had tasted it, He would not drink. {Mt}

It was the third hour when they crucified Him. {Mk} With Him they crucified two others, one on either side, “and Jesus in the center.” {Jn} Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.” {Lk}

The soldiers divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier. His tunic was without seam, woven in one piece from the top, so they said among themselves, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be.” So the Scripture was fulfilled: “They divided My garments among them, And for My clothing they cast lots.” {Jn} Then they sat down and kept watch over Him there. {Mt}

Pilate had written a title and put it on the cross: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. Many read it, because the place was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. The chief priests asked Pilate to change it to say only that Jesus claimed to be King of the Jews. Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.” {Jn}

Those who passed by blasphemed Him, wagging their heads: “You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save Yourself!” {Mt} The chief priests mocked with the scribes and elders: “He saved others; Himself He cannot save.” “He trusted in God; let Him deliver Him now if He will have Him.” {Mt} The soldiers mocked Him too, offering Him sour wine and saying, “If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself.” {Lk} Even the robbers crucified with Him reviled Him. {Mk}

One of the criminals hanging there blasphemed Him: “If You are the Christ, save Yourself and us.” But the other rebuked him: “Do you not even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation?” He added that they were receiving what their deeds deserved, “but this Man has done nothing wrong.” Then he said, “Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.” Jesus answered, “Assuredly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” {Lk}

Near the cross stood His mother, and His mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing by, He said to her, “Woman, behold your son!” Then He said to the disciple, “Behold your mother!” And from that hour that disciple took her to his own home. {Jn}
differences: The title reads “THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Matthew), “THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Mark), “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Luke) and “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS” (John). Luke and John say it was written in three languages.
Matthew says they offered sour wine mingled with gall; Mark says wine mingled with myrrh. Only Mark gives the hour, “the third hour.”
Matthew and Mark say both robbers reviled Jesus. Luke says one blasphemed Him while the other rebuked him and turned to Jesus.
Only Luke records the prayer “Father, forgive them” and the promise of Paradise. Only John records the seamless tunic, the chief priests’ complaint about the title and Jesus’ words to His mother.
Matthew alone records the taunt “He trusted in God”; Luke alone says the soldiers mocked Him by offering sour wine.

fit.question: The four Gospels give the wording of the sign on the cross four different ways. What did it actually say?

points.label: Three languages
points.text: Luke and John say the title was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. The wording need not have been identical in each language, and different witnesses may have read or remembered different versions.

points.label: The same charge
points.text: All four agree on the heart of it: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” That was the charge for which Jesus died. Each writer gives the essential words; taken together, the accounts suggest a full form something like This is Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.

fit.note: Witnesses who agree on the charge but vary in wording are what honest reporting looks like. No account contradicts another.
fit.short: The sign was written in three languages, and each writer gives its essential charge: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

fit.question: Mark says Jesus was crucified at “the third hour,” about nine in the morning. John says Pilate was still giving his verdict at “about the sixth hour” (John 19:14), about noon. How can both be true?

points.label: Hours told roughly
points.text: Without clocks, people marked the day in blocks: the third, sixth and ninth hours, the same marks the Gospels use for the darkness and the death. John says “about” the sixth hour. A time in the late morning could be called the third hour by one witness, naming the block it fell in, and about the sixth by another, rounding toward noon. Many evangelical scholars hold some form of this view.

points.label: A different count
points.text: Others, McGarvey among them, think John counted the hours from midnight, so that “about the sixth hour” means about six in the morning, with the crucifixion following at nine. But John’s other times of day (1:39; 4:6; 4:52) read most naturally from sunrise, and whether a midnight count was used in John’s day is debated.

fit.note: Faithful scholars weigh these answers differently, but both writers place the crucifixion on Friday morning after a night of trials, and neither requires an error.
fit.short: Hours were reckoned roughly, so late morning could fit both “third” and “about the sixth”; or John counted from midnight.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark say both robbers reviled Jesus. Luke says one mocked Him and the other defended Him. Which is it?

points.label: A change of heart
points.text: Jesus hung on the cross for hours. Both men may have joined the mockery at first, as Matthew and Mark report, and later one of them stopped, rebuked the other and turned to Jesus. Luke tells that later moment.

points.label: Speaking of a group
points.text: Matthew and Mark may also be speaking of the robbers as a group, the way the soldiers or the passersby are described together, while Luke gives the closer view of two different men.

fit.note: Luke explains rather than contradicts the others: a man who began by mocking ended by praying.
fit.short: Both robbers mocked at first; during the long hours on the cross one of them changed and turned to Jesus.

scene.label: Golgotha
scene.text: The Aramaic name means skull. No one knows whether it came from the shape of the ground or from executions there. It lay outside the city but near it (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12), where people passed by (Matthew 27:39). Since the fourth century the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has marked the traditional site, which was outside the wall in Jesus’ day.

scene.label: Crucifixion
scene.text: Rome kept crucifixion for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. The condemned man was nailed or tied to the cross (John 20:25 speaks of “the print of the nails”) and left to die slowly in public, often over many hours, as strength and breath failed. The Gospels do not describe the agony. They say simply, “they crucified Him.”

scene.label: Three languages
scene.text: Hebrew here probably means Aramaic, the everyday speech of the Jews. Latin was the language of Roman rule, and Greek the common language of the eastern empire. The charge was posted in the main languages of the crowds at the feast.

scene.label: Psalm 22
scene.text: The mockers did not know they were acting out a psalm. Psalm 22 describes those who “shake the head” and say, “He trusted in the LORD, let Him rescue Him” (22:7–8), and men who divide the sufferer’s garments by lot (22:18).

scene.label: Paradise
scene.text: The word comes from a Persian term for a walled garden or park. The Greek Old Testament used it for the garden of Eden, and Jews of Jesus’ day used it for the place of blessing for the righteous dead. Paul says he was “caught up into Paradise” (2 Corinthians 12:4).

witnesses.matthew: Matthew stresses the mockery and the fulfillment of Scripture. The rulers’ taunt, “He trusted in God,” echoes Psalm 22:8, and the passersby’s challenge, “If You are the Son of God,” repeats the tempter’s words in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3, 6).
witnesses.mark: Mark gives the hour and the bare facts. In Mark, Jesus says nothing during these hours: He refuses the drugged wine and endures the mockery in silence, the Servant who “opened not His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).
witnesses.luke: Luke records two sayings no one else gives: the prayer for forgiveness and the promise of Paradise. In Luke the cross is still a place where Jesus forgives and receives a sinner, and where a condemned man becomes one more witness that Jesus “has done nothing wrong.”
witnesses.john: John, who stood near the cross, records the title in three languages, Pilate’s refusal to change it, the seamless tunic and Jesus’ care for His mother. He notes Scripture fulfilled even in the soldiers’ casting of lots.

seeing.reveals: The sign meant as mockery told the truth: Jesus is the King of the Jews, and He reigns by giving Himself. He could not save Himself and save others too, and He chose others.
seeing.living: The criminal had nothing to offer: no time left, no good works, no way to make amends. He asked only to be remembered, and Jesus promised him Paradise “today.” Come to Jesus with the same empty hands, and do not count anyone too far gone for Him.
seeing.ponder: Which voice is closer to your own heart: “save Yourself,” or “Lord, remember me”?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus would not save Himself, so that He could save others.
outline: A criminal who asked to be remembered (40–42)
preaching.watch_for: Luke repeats the taunt three times: the rulers (v. 35), the soldiers (v. 37) and the criminal (v. 39) all tell Jesus to save Himself. The sermon turns on why He did not.
